doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

chapter: Drumming concepts and jazz as a word
title: Competitive jam sessions with Roy Eldridge; self-taught southern players
summary: Music was like sports; he and Eldridge hunted jam sessions to cut people, and southern players developed individual styles by trial and error.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Do different musicians that play different ways ‘cause you to react certain ways as a drummer?

Well yes. I am very competitive. In fact when I worked with Roy Eldridge, he was of the same mentality. And we used to go out and look for jam sessions and look for guys to cut you know. Because back then it was just like sports. I mean music was like sports. You and I can be the best of friends. And you play drums, I play drums. But when we got on the bandstand it was a different ball game. Everything went out the window. I mean I’m competing with you and you are competing with me. And that’s why, you know, there were so many new ideas and things that was going on and everybody had their own individual style, because they were themselves. You know they didn’t study with someone that everybody has to do it the same way. I mean like in the south a lot of the musicians, they didn’t have any music teachers. They learned by trial and errors. So you might see a guy that’s a trumpet player, and he’d have both jaws out like this you know, like Dizzy Gillespie. That’s because I mean when he started out he didn’t have nobody to tell him that that was wrong. But he got results doing this.
